engRhHs: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets…" — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is used?
Anaphora (repetition at the start of clauses)
Churchill repeats "we shall fight" at the start of each clause to build determination.
"Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." — John F. Kennedy (1961). Which strategy is used?
Kennedy reverses "you" and "your country" in the second half, which is chiasmus.
"A house divided against itself cannot stand." — Abraham Lincoln (1858), speaking of a nation split over slavery. Which strategy is used?
Lincoln compares the divided nation to a house, without using "like" or "as."
"Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?" — Patrick Henry (1775). Which strategy is used?
Henry asks a question he expects no one to answer "yes" to, to make his point.
"Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is most prominent?
Churchill places the opposites "so many" and "so few" side by side for effect.
"I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat." — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is used?
Churchill lists four vivid images of hardship to prepare listeners for sacrifice.
"With malice toward none, with charity for all…" — Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (1865). Which strategy is used?
Both phrases follow the pattern "with ___ toward/for ___" while contrasting "none" and "all."
"I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king." — Queen Elizabeth I (1588). Which strategy is used?
Concession followed by a contrasting claim
Elizabeth first grants a perceived weakness, then turns it with "but" to assert her strength.
"Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963). Which strategy is used?
"Let every nation know… that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe…" — John F. Kennedy (1961). Which strategy is used?
Parallel structure in a series of verb phrases
Each phrase follows the same verb + "any" + noun pattern, building rhythm and resolve.
"Give me liberty, or give me death!" — Patrick Henry (1775). Which strategy is used?
Henry presents only two extreme options to show how much he values liberty.
"We refuse to believe that the bank of justice is bankrupt." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963), continuing his image of a promissory note. Which strategy is used?
King develops the comparison of America's promises to a cheque across several sentences.
"From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent." — Winston Churchill (1946). Which strategy is used?
Churchill describes the division of Europe as an "iron curtain," a metaphor for a hard barrier.
"Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation…" — Abraham Lincoln (1863). What is the main effect of beginning this way?
It recalls the nation's founding in solemn, formal language
It gives a precise statistic about battles
It tells a humorous personal story
Counting back to 1776 in biblical-sounding language reminds listeners of the founding ideals.
Frederick Douglass asked an 1852 audience, "What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July?" What was the main purpose of this question?
To expose the hypocrisy of celebrating freedom while slavery existed
To ask for directions to the celebration
To introduce a statistic about July
The question forces listeners to confront the gap between their ideals of liberty and the reality of slavery.
"The only thing we have to fear is fear itself." — Franklin D. Roosevelt (1933), during the Great Depression. What was the main purpose of this line?
To calm a frightened public and discourage panic
To list the causes of the Depression
Roosevelt reframes fear itself as the danger, urging Americans not to give in to panic.
"It was we, the people; not we, the white male citizens; nor yet we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed the Union." — Susan B. Anthony (1873). Which strategy is used?
Repetition of a famous phrase to redefine it
Anthony repeats "we, the people" from the Constitution to argue it includes women.
"Ich bin ein Berliner" ("I am a Berliner"). — John F. Kennedy, speaking in West Berlin (1963). What strategy does this line mainly use?
Identifying with the audience to show solidarity
Using sarcasm to mock the crowd
Telling a story about his childhood
By declaring himself a Berliner in their language, Kennedy aligns himself with his listeners.
"Never retract, never explain, never apologize — get the thing done and let them howl." — attributed to Nellie McClung. Which strategy is used?
The repeated "never" at the start of each phrase creates a forceful rhythm.
A wartime speaker calls a devastating defeat "a setback of some inconvenience." Which strategy is this?
Describing a devastating loss in mild terms deliberately downplays it.
"Let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963). Which strategy is used?
Anaphora (repetition at the start of sentences)
Each sentence begins with "Let freedom ring," building momentum across the speech's ending.
A nineteenth-century speaker opens, "I speak to you not as a politician, but as a mother who has buried two sons in this war." Which appeal does this mainly establish?
Ethos and pathos through personal experience
Her personal loss gives her credibility and stirs the audience's emotions.

engCmpP: Which sentence is correct and clear?

Which sentence is correct and clear?
Of the three runners, Priya is the fastest.
Of the three runners, Priya is the faster.
Of the three runners, Priya is the most fastest.
Of the three runners, Priya is more fast.
Use the superlative "fastest" when comparing three or more.

Between the two essays, Leah's is the stronger.
Between the two essays, Leah's is the strongest.
Between the two essays, Leah's is the most strong.
Between the two essays, Leah's is more stronger.

The Rockies are higher than any mountains in Canada.

This year's results were worse than last year's.

This is the most unusual design I have seen.

The second test was less difficult than the first.
The second test was less difficulter than the first.

The new phone's battery lasts more longer than the old phone's.

An article title appears in quotation marks right after the author.
Entry: Tremblay, Luc. "Saving the Monarchs." Canadian Geographic, vol. 141, no. 2, 2021, pp. 30–37. What is the container?
The container is the larger publication, here the italicized magazine title.
Entry: Tremblay, Luc. "Saving the Monarchs." Canadian Geographic, vol. 141, no. 2, 2021, pp. 30–37. What is the volume number?
The volume number follows the abbreviation vol.
Entry: Tremblay, Luc. "Saving the Monarchs." Canadian Geographic, vol. 141, no. 2, 2021, pp. 30–37. Which issue number is given?
The issue number follows the abbreviation no.
Entry: Tremblay, Luc. "Saving the Monarchs." Canadian Geographic, vol. 141, no. 2, 2021, pp. 30–37. Which pages does the article cover?
pp. 30–37 shows the article runs from page 30 to page 37.
Entry: Singh, Priya. "How Glaciers Move." Earth Now, 4 Mar. 2022, www.earthnow.ca/glaciers. What does www.earthnow.ca/glaciers show?
The location (web address) of the source
For an online source, MLA ends the entry with the URL as its location.
Entry: Singh, Priya. "How Glaciers Move." Earth Now, 4 Mar. 2022, www.earthnow.ca/glaciers. When was the article published?
MLA writes dates day, month, year, so 4 Mar. 2022 means 4 March 2022.
Entry: Singh, Priya. "How Glaciers Move." Earth Now, 4 Mar. 2022, www.earthnow.ca/glaciers. What is the name of the website?
The italicized name after the article title is the website, which is the container.
Entry: Morales, Ana, and Ben Wright. Coding for Beginners. 2nd ed., Pearson, 2019. How many authors does the book have?
Two authors are joined by and; only the first is written last name first.

It is the second edition of the book
ed. after an ordinal number shows which edition of the book is cited.
Entry: Morales, Ana, and Ben Wright. Coding for Beginners. 2nd ed., Pearson, 2019. Why is the second author written Ben Wright rather than Wright, Ben?
Only the first author's name is reversed
The second author is the editor

Entry: Okafor, Ngozi. Rivers of the North. House of Anansi, 2018. Where would this entry be placed in the Works Cited list?
Works Cited entries are alphabetized by the first word, which is usually the author's last name.
Entry: "Wildfire Season Begins." CBC News, 2 June 2023. Why does this entry begin with the article title?
When there is no author, MLA starts the entry with the title of the source.

Shorter works within a larger container, like articles, go in quotation marks.
In MLA format, how is the title of a website shown when it is the container?
Containers, such as websites, magazines and books, are italicized.
What is the title at the top of an MLA list of sources?
MLA names the list Works Cited and centres the title at the top of the page.
How are lines after the first one in each MLA Works Cited entry formatted?
Indented half an inch (a hanging indent)
MLA uses a hanging indent so each entry's first word stands out.
Which punctuation mark follows the author's name in an MLA Works Cited entry?
The author element ends with a period, as in Okafor, Ngozi.
Entry: Patel, Ravi. The Last Ice. Nimbus, 2020. Which entry would come right before it in an alphabetical list?
Lee begins with L, which comes before P in alphabetical order, while the others come after.

In this entry, what is vol. 134? Bauer, Kim. "The Science of Sleep." Maclean's, vol. 134, no. 5, 2021, pp. 22–25.

The italicized website name is the container that holds the article.

For online sources, the URL is the location element at the end of the entry.
In this entry, what is 10 Jan. 2023? Ahmed, Sara. "Northern Lights Explained." Sky Watch, 10 Jan. 2023, www.skywatch.ca/aurora.
The date after the container shows when the web article was published.
In this entry, what is "Northern Lights Explained"? Ahmed, Sara. "Northern Lights Explained." Sky Watch, 10 Jan. 2023, www.skywatch.ca/aurora.
The title of the web page appears in quotation marks.
In this entry, what is editor? Clark, Joe, editor. Voices of the Coast. Harbour Publishing, 2015.
A label showing Joe Clark edited the book rather than wrote it
In MLA, a descriptor such as editor follows the name of a person who edited the work.
In this entry, what is Harbour Publishing? Clark, Joe, editor. Voices of the Coast. Harbour Publishing, 2015.
The publisher appears before the year in a book entry.
In this entry, what is Translated by Tom Hill? Dubois, Marie. Le Petit Prince Revisited. Translated by Tom Hill, Orca, 2020.
MLA lists other contributors, such as translators, after the title.

The person whose name begins the entry is the author of the work.
In this entry, what is Orca? Dubois, Marie. Le Petit Prince Revisited. Translated by Tom Hill, Orca, 2020.
The publisher appears just before the year.
In MLA 8th edition, what is a container?
The larger work that holds the source
The page range of the source
The date you accessed the source
A container is the larger whole, such as a magazine, website or anthology, that includes the source.
Which list shows the first MLA core elements in the correct order?
Author, title of source, title of container
MLA core elements begin with author, then title of source, then title of container.
In this entry, which element comes immediately after "Ocean Plastics"? Smith, Alex. "Ocean Plastics." Science Weekly, vol. 12, no. 3, 2021, pp. 14–19.
After the title of the source, MLA lists the title of the container.
engInTx: You quote page 112 of a book by Bergeron. Which MLA in-text citation is correct?
MLA puts the author's last name and page number with no comma or p. between them.
You paraphrase page 7 of an article by Tanaka. Which citation is correct?
Paraphrases are cited the same way as quotations: last name and page number.
The author is named in your sentence: Desai argues that … The idea is on page 30. What goes in the parentheses?
When the author is named in the sentence, only the page number goes in the parentheses.
A source has three or more authors: Kim, Ortiz and Walsh. You cite page 9. Which citation is correct?
For three or more authors, MLA uses the first author's last name followed by et al.
A website has no author. Its page title is "Bee Facts". Which citation is correct?
With no author, MLA uses a shortened title in quotation marks.
A book with no author is titled The Great Canadian Atlas. You cite page 50. Which citation is correct?
A book title stays italicized in a citation, shortened to its key words, followed by the page.
You cite two different books by Atwood. Which citation makes clear which book you mean?
When you cite more than one work by the same author, add a short title after a comma.
You quote two authors named Lee (Jordan Lee and Ming Lee). Which citation is correct?
When two cited authors share a last name, add the first initial to tell them apart.
Which sentence places the in-text citation correctly?
The ice is melting faster than expected (Ross 22).
The ice is melting faster than expected. (Ross 22)
(Ross 22) The ice is melting faster than expected.
The ice is (Ross 22) melting faster than expected.
The parenthetical citation goes at the end of the borrowed idea, before the period.
A quotation ends with a question mark: "Who decides?" Where does the citation go?
Keep the question mark inside the quotation marks, then add the citation and a period.
What should every in-text citation match?
The first word of an entry in the Works Cited list
The first sentence of the source
The date you read the source
The name or title in parentheses lets readers find the matching Works Cited entry.
You cite pages 40 to 42 of a book by Fraser. Which citation is correct?
Page ranges use a dash between the numbers and no pp.
You quote a line from an online video by the National Film Board, which shows 02:15 as the time. Which citation is correct?
For time-based media, MLA gives the time stamp in place of a page number.
A source is written by a group, the Canadian Red Cross, with no page numbers. Which citation is correct?
A corporate author is cited by its name, and no page is given when the source has none.
You quote a long passage of more than four lines. How should it be formatted?
As an indented block quotation with the citation after the final period
In quotation marks with the citation before the period
As a footnote at the bottom of the page
Long quotations are set off as block quotations, and the citation follows the closing punctuation.
The author is named in your sentence: As Kovač explains, … The source is a web page with no page numbers. What goes in the parentheses?
Nothing; no parenthetical citation is needed
If the author is named in the sentence and there is no page number, no parentheses are needed.
You quote a poem by Pauline Johnson and cite lines 5 to 7. Which citation is correct?
For poems, MLA cites line numbers; write lines the first time to make that clear.
You cite a quotation that Sharma used, originally said by Lin, on page 61 of Sharma's book. Which citation is correct?
For an indirect source, use qtd. in with the author of the source you actually read.
Why do writers use in-text citations?
To give credit to sources and help readers find them
To show the essay's word count
To replace the Works Cited list
In-text citations credit borrowed ideas and point readers to full entries in the Works Cited list.
Which in-text citation uses correct MLA punctuation?
MLA puts only a space between the author's name and the page number.
You cite two sources for the same idea: Grant page 5 and Shah page 19. Which citation is correct?
Multiple sources in one parenthetical citation are separated by a semicolon.
You quote two authors, Murphy and Bell, page 3. Which citation is correct?
For two authors, MLA names both, joined by and.
engWpAn: Complete the analogy. paint : painter :: garden : ___
Adding -er to a verb names the person who does it, so garden becomes gardener.
Complete the analogy. fear : fearless :: help : ___
-less means without, so without help is helpless.
Complete the analogy. joy : joyful :: peace : ___
-ful means full of, so full of peace is peaceful.
Complete the analogy. happy : happiness :: lonely : ___
-ness turns an adjective into a noun, and the y changes to i.
Complete the analogy. legal : illegal :: logical : ___
Before a word starting with l, the negative prefix in- becomes il-.
Complete the analogy. possible : impossible :: patient : ___
Complete the analogy. regular : irregular :: responsible : ___
Complete the analogy. connect : disconnect :: obey : ___
dis- reverses or negates a verb, so obey becomes disobey.
Complete the analogy. spell : misspell :: understand : ___
mis- means wrongly, so to understand wrongly is to misunderstand.
Complete the analogy. view : preview :: heat : ___
pre- means before, matching preview, which means to view beforehand.
Complete the analogy. move : movement :: govern : ___
-ment turns a verb into a noun naming the action or result, like movement.
Complete the analogy. decide : decision :: divide : ___
Verbs ending in -ide often form nouns ending in -ision.
Complete the analogy. read : readable :: wash : ___
-able means able to be, so able to be washed is washable.
Complete the analogy. child : childhood :: neighbour : ___
-hood names a state or group, like childhood and neighbourhood.
Complete the analogy. friend : friendship :: leader : ___
-ship names a state or role, so friend becomes friendship and leader becomes leadership.
Complete the analogy. wide : widen :: short : ___
-en turns an adjective into a verb meaning to make, so to make short is to shorten.
Complete the analogy. modern : modernize :: visual : ___
-ize turns an adjective into a verb; Canadian spelling keeps the z.
Complete the analogy. cycle : bicycle :: angle : ___
Numeric prefixes follow a pattern: bi- for two in bicycle, tri- for three in triangle.
Complete the analogy. danger : dangerous :: fame : ___
-ous means full of; the silent e in fame is dropped.
Complete the analogy. science : scientist :: art : ___
-ist names a person who practises something, like scientist and artist.
Complete the analogy. marine : submarine :: way : ___
sub- means under, so a subway runs under the ground as a submarine goes under the sea.
Complete the analogy. courage : encourage :: danger : ___
en- turns a noun into a verb meaning to put into, so to put in danger is to endanger.

ir- means not and -able means able to be, so irreplaceable means not able to be replaced.

re- means again, so renew means to make new again.

engFgEt: Biology comes from Greek bios ("life") + logia ("study"). What does biology mean?
a book about a person's life
Combining life and study gives the study of living things.
Telephone comes from Greek tele ("far") + phone ("sound, voice"). What is a telephone?
a device that carries voices over a distance
a tool for seeing far away
Far plus voice describes a device that sends voices over a distance.
Benevolent comes from Latin bene ("well") + volens ("wishing"). What does benevolent mean?
Wishing well describes a kind, generous person.
Malnutrition comes from Latin mal ("bad") + nutrire ("to nourish"). What does malnutrition mean?
poor nourishment from a lack of healthy food
Bad nourishment means the body lacks the food it needs.
Chronological comes from Greek chronos ("time") + logos ("word, reason"). What does chronological order mean?
arranged in the order events happened in time
The root chronos points to time, so chronological order follows time.
Democracy comes from Greek demos ("people") + kratos ("power, rule"). What is a democracy?
People plus rule means a system where citizens hold power.
Manuscript comes from Latin manu ("by hand") + scriptus ("written"). What is a manuscript, originally?
Written by hand describes a handwritten document.
Submarine comes from Latin sub ("under") + marinus ("of the sea"). What is a submarine?
a vessel that travels under the sea
a boat that floats on rivers
Under plus sea describes a vessel that operates underwater.
Autograph comes from Greek autos ("self") + graphein ("to write"). What is an autograph?
Self plus write means something a person writes themselves, like a signature.
Insomnia comes from Latin in ("not") + somnus ("sleep"). What is insomnia?
Not plus sleep describes difficulty sleeping.
Hydrophobia comes from Greek hydor ("water") + phobos ("fear"). What does hydrophobia mean?
Water plus fear gives a fear of water.
Philanthropist comes from Greek philos ("loving") + anthropos ("human being"). What is a philanthropist?
a person who gives to help others
A lover of humanity is someone who generously helps others.
Circumference comes from Latin circum ("around") + ferre ("to carry"). What is the circumference of a circle?
Carried around describes the distance around the outside of a circle.
Malevolent comes from Latin male ("badly") + volens ("wishing"). What does malevolent mean?
Wishing badly means wanting harm to come to others.
Unanimous comes from Latin unus ("one") + animus ("mind"). What does a unanimous vote mean?
One mind means everyone thinks the same.
Astronaut comes from Greek astron ("star") + nautes ("sailor"). What is an astronaut?
a person trained to travel in space
A star sailor is someone who travels into space.
Spectator comes from Latin spectare ("to watch"). What is a spectator?
a person who watches an event
a person who plays in a game
Someone who watches is a spectator.
Credible comes from Latin credere ("to believe"). What does credible mean?
From to believe, credible describes something believable.
Pedestrian comes from Latin pedes ("on foot"). What is a pedestrian?
On foot describes a person who is walking.
Ambiguous comes from Latin ambi ("both ways") + agere ("to drive, lead"). What does ambiguous mean?
open to more than one meaning
Leading both ways describes something that can be understood in more than one way.
Sympathy comes from Greek syn ("together") + pathos ("feeling"). What is sympathy?
Feeling together means sharing someone else's sorrow or feelings.
Companion comes from Latin com ("with") + panis ("bread"). What is a companion?
a person you spend time with
Originally someone you share bread with, a companion is someone who keeps you company.
engFgCx: What does the expression in bold mean? After the long winter, the first warm day gave everyone a feeling of joie de vivre, and the park filled with laughing families.
The laughing families in the park show a cheerful delight in living.

If the restaurant would close without her, she is its reason for existing.

The sunglasses and hat show he hid his identity.

an impressive achievement showing great skill
Calling it the finest book of the year shows it was a masterful achievement.

The cousins met at that spot, so it is a meeting place.

What does the expression in bold mean? The new student felt a bit of déjà vu, sure she had walked down this exact hallway before.
the feeling of having already experienced something

What does the expression in bold mean? The fashion show's designs were avant-garde, unlike anything the audience had seen.

The statement came after the story spread, so post hoc means after the fact.
What does the expression in bold mean? He was the enfant terrible of the art world, always shocking critics with outrageous work.
a person whose unconventional behaviour shocks others

What does the expression in bold mean? We agreed on a quid pro quo: I would help with her math homework, and she would help me with French.
a favour given in return for another
Each person helps the other, so it is an exchange of favours.
What does the expression in bold mean? At the end of the meal, the waiter asked if we wanted dessert à la mode, with a scoop of vanilla ice cream on the pie.

engFLC: Which logical fallacy is this? My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking can't be that harmful.
It draws a broad conclusion from a single example.
Which logical fallacy is this? A famous hockey player says this cereal is the healthiest, so it must be.
A hockey player is not an expert on nutrition, so citing him is an improper appeal to authority.
Which logical fallacy is this? The book is true because it says so in the book.
The conclusion is used as its own evidence.
Which logical fallacy is this? I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks caused the win.
It assumes that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
Which logical fallacy is this? Why worry about my late assignment when there are so many problems in the world?
It distracts from the real issue by changing the subject.
Which logical fallacy is this? If we allow one extra day for this assignment, students will expect extensions on every test, and soon nobody will meet any deadline.
It claims one small step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences.
Which logical fallacy is this? All my friends have their ears pierced, so I should too.
It argues something is right because many people are doing it.
Which logical fallacy is this? My opponent wants to reduce the military budget, so he obviously wants to leave the country defenceless.
It distorts the opponent's position into an extreme version that is easier to attack.
Which logical fallacy is this? Don't listen to his ideas about recycling — he drives an old truck.
It attacks the person instead of addressing his argument.
Which logical fallacy is this? You either support the new stadium or you don't care about this city.
It presents only two options when many other positions exist.
Which logical fallacy is this? I met two rude people from that town, so everyone there must be rude.
It judges an entire group based on a tiny sample.
Which logical fallacy is this? Ever since the new principal arrived, it has rained more. She must be bad luck.
It mistakes a coincidence in timing for cause and effect.
Which logical fallacy is this? She is a trustworthy leader because she is honest, and we know she is honest because she is trustworthy.
The argument goes in a circle, using each claim to prove the other.
Which logical fallacy is this? Sure, our factory polluted the river, but think of all the jobs we create!
It shifts attention away from the pollution to an unrelated benefit.
Which logical fallacy is this? A popular actor says this vitamin cures colds, so it must work.
An actor's fame does not make them an expert on medicine.
Which logical fallacy is this? If we ban phones in class, next they'll ban talking, and soon school will be like a prison.
It assumes a chain of extreme events will follow from one rule.
Which logical fallacy is this? The environmentalists want us to protect the wetlands, so they clearly want to stop all farming forever.
It exaggerates the opponents' view into one they do not hold.
Which logical fallacy is this? Either you join the debate club or you'll never learn to speak in public.
It ignores the many other ways to learn public speaking.
Which logical fallacy is this? This video has ten million views, so the information in it must be accurate.
Popularity does not prove that information is true.
Which logical fallacy is this? Why should we believe her science report? She failed gym class.
It attacks an unrelated personal trait instead of the report itself.
Which logical fallacy is this? After I started drinking green tea, I got better marks, so green tea makes you smarter.
It assumes the tea caused the better marks just because it came first.
Which logical fallacy is this? The first two episodes of the series were boring, so the whole series must be terrible.
It reaches a sweeping conclusion from limited evidence.

She is excited to retire from her job

engRHD: Which device is used? “… government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.” — Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address (1863)
The phrase the people is repeated at the end of successive phrases.
Which device is used? The view from the summit was not unimpressive.
Litotes makes a point by denying its opposite (not unimpressive means impressive).
Which device is used? We laughed and sang and danced and talked until dawn.
Polysyndeton repeats conjunctions such as and between items.
Which device is used? She was tired, hungry, cold, alone.
Asyndeton leaves out the conjunctions between items in a series.
Which device is used? Eat to live; do not live to eat.
Chiasmus reverses the order of words in two parallel phrases.
Which device is used? This backpack weighs a tonne!
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Which device is used? Who among us does not want clean water for our children?
The question is asked for effect, not to get an answer.
Which device is used? It was an open secret that the coach would retire.
Which device is used? The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know.
A paradox seems contradictory but reveals a truth.
Which device is used? Every day we wait, every day we hesitate, every day we lose ground.
The phrase every day is repeated at the start of each clause.
Which device is used? “To err is human; to forgive, divine.” — Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)
Antithesis places contrasting ideas side by side in parallel structure.
Which device is used? “When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child …” — 1 Corinthians 13:11, King James Bible (1611)
The phrase as a child is repeated at the end of each clause.
Which device is used? Bold, bright and beautiful beginnings await you.
Which device is used? On a 40-degree day, Ravi wiped his forehead and said, “It's a bit warm.”
Understatement deliberately makes something seem less extreme than it is.
Which device is used? Don't open that Pandora's box by bringing up the old argument.
An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known story, here a Greek myth.
Which device is used? “Death, be not proud …” — John Donne, Holy Sonnet 10 (1633)
Apostrophe directly addresses something absent or non-human, here Death.
Which device is used? Ottawa announced new funding for rural schools today.
Metonymy uses a related term, the capital city, to stand for the federal government.
Which device is used? Sadly, our old dog passed away last spring.
Passed away is a gentler way of saying died.
Which device is used? Are we really going to let a little rain stop us?
The speaker asks the question to make a point, not to get an answer.
Which device is used? “I must be cruel only to be kind.” — William Shakespeare, Hamlet (c. 1600)
Being cruel in order to be kind seems contradictory but expresses a truth.
Which device is used? Never let your fear decide your future; let your future decide your fear.
The words fear and future are reversed in the second clause.
Which device is used? Lily joined the team because she loves running, enjoys competing and wants to improve.
The reasons share the same grammatical structure (verb plus object).
